title: Hubble’s View of NGC 5584
caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 5584, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 5584 · constellation Virgo · about About 72 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, A. Riess (STScI/JHU), L. Macri (Texas A&M University), and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Blue light from young stars traces the graceful spiral arms of NGC 5584, and thin dark dust lanes seem to flow out from its yellowish core, where older stars live. The reddish dots scattered across the frame are mostly background galaxies. NGC 5584 lies about 72 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

Its stars include pulsating Cepheid variables, and it recently hosted a Type Ia supernova, a special class of exploding star. A Cepheid pulsates at a rate closely tied to its true brightness, which makes it a good distance marker for relatively nearby galaxies. Type Ia supernovae all flare with the same brightness and can be seen much farther away.

Comparing the two kinds of star in the same galaxy lets astronomers calibrate supernovae in distant galaxies and work out how far away those galaxies are. NGC 5584 was one of eight galaxies used in this way, with more than 600 Cepheids analysed in total, 250 of them here. The work measured how fast the universe is expanding today with an uncertainty of just 3.3 percent.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3 took this image in visible light. NASA shows F350LP in white, F555W in blue and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The exposures add up to 20.8 hours, gathering far more light than the eye could, enough to pick out individual pulsating stars in another galaxy.

explore: The team, led by Adam Riess of the Space Telescope Science Institute and Johns Hopkins University, found an expansion rate of 73.8 kilometers per second per megaparsec. That ruled out the idea that we live near the centre of a huge bubble of relatively empty space, an alternative explanation for the apparent acceleration usually attributed to dark energy.
sources: NASA release: NASA’s Hubble Rules Out One Alternative to Dark Energy
